claim: Training method achieves 94% accuracy on CIFAR-10 in 3.29 seconds
conditions: CIFAR-10 dataset, single NVIDIA A100 GPU
effect: 94% top-1 accuracy achieved in 3.29 seconds wall-clock time
evidence: Direct experimental result stated in abstract
quote: training methods for CIFAR-10 which reach 94% accuracy in 3.29 seconds
paper: 94% on CIFAR-10 in 3.29 Seconds on a Single GPU

claim: Derandomized horizontal flipping augmentation improves over standard flipping augmentation
conditions: CIFAR-10 dataset, scenarios where horizontal flipping is beneficial
effect: Improvement over standard horizontal flipping method in all cases where flipping is beneficial
evidence: Empirical comparison in paper's augmentation experiments
quote: we propose a derandomized variant of horizontal flipping augmentation, which we show improves over the standard method in every case where flipping is beneficial over no flipping at all
paper: 94% on CIFAR-10 in 3.29 Seconds on a Single GPU

claim: Smooth learning rate schedules outperform constant rates and calendar-based decay schedules
conditions: Image classification (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10); 4 architecture families (fully connected, convolutional, recurrent, residual); 72 runs; fixed optimizer, data pipeline, and evaluation protocol
effect: 2.5 percentage points on CIFAR-10 dataset mean; margins grow with task difficulty
evidence: Comparative empirical benchmark across multiple datasets and architectures
quote: Schedules that fall smoothly from peak to floor beat the constant rate and calendar-based decay by margins that grow with task difficulty, reaching 2.5 points of dataset mean on CIFAR-10.
paper: BrachistoneLR: A Brachistochrone-Inspired Learning-Rate Schedule and a Controlled Benchmark of Scheduling Policies

claim: BrachistoneLR, cosine annealing, and warmup-cosine schedules achieve statistically indistinguishable performance
conditions: CIFAR-10; one seed per configuration; residual networks and other architectures tested
effect: Performance gap within 0.06 accuracy points and 0.17 of mean rank; insufficient statistical power to separate with single seed
evidence: Empirical benchmark comparison across 72 runs
quote: BrachistoneLR, cosine annealing, and warmup-cosine lie within 0.06 accuracy points and 0.17 of a mean rank, which one seed per configuration cannot separate.
paper: BrachistoneLR: A Brachistochrone-Inspired Learning-Rate Schedule and a Controlled Benchmark of Scheduling Policies

claim: The shape of a learning rate schedule matters more than its specific parameterization
conditions: Image classification across MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10; 4 architecture families
effect: The choice to use a smooth schedule is more consequential than tuning milestones, decay factors, warmup length, or restart periods
evidence: Empirical observation from comparative benchmarking study
quote: the shape of a schedule matters more than its parameterization, that the choice of whether to use a smooth schedule matters more than the choice among them
paper: BrachistoneLR: A Brachistochrone-Inspired Learning-Rate Schedule and a Controlled Benchmark of Scheduling Policies

claim: Terminal-rate effects of learning rate schedules decay rapidly with epoch budget and are negligible for practical training horizons
conditions: Asymptotic analysis of schedule endpoints; short to moderate training horizons
effect: E^−2 decay rate; not worth attention beyond short horizons
evidence: Theoretical analysis; empirical observation that the 1-epoch terminal-rate shift is only worth attention over short horizons
quote: the terminal-rate distinction is worth attention only over short horizons.
paper: BrachistoneLR: A Brachistochrone-Inspired Learning-Rate Schedule and a Controlled Benchmark of Scheduling Policies

claim: BrachistoneLR achieves best performance on residual networks and highest CIFAR-10 accuracy among tested schedules
conditions: CIFAR-10; residual networks; benchmark of 6 schedules across 72 runs
effect: Best performance among BrachistoneLR, cosine annealing, warmup-cosine, and other schedule baselines
evidence: Empirical benchmark result
quote: BrachistoneLR is best on both residual networks and has the highest CIFAR-10 mean
paper: BrachistoneLR: A Brachistochrone-Inspired Learning-Rate Schedule and a Controlled Benchmark of Scheduling Policies

claim: The choice of learning rate scheduler depends heavily on the architecture
conditions: 30 representative architectures (CNNs and transformers), 25 scheduler configurations, CIFAR-10 classification, 3,938 model variants evaluated
effect: Architecture-scheduler interaction is a primary determinant of final accuracy
evidence: Systematic empirical evaluation across diverse architecture families showing differential scheduler performance
quote: The results show that the choice of scheduler depends heavily on the architecture: CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts and CyclicLR consistently outperform basic decay strategies.
paper: Systematic Evaluation of Learning Rate Scheduling Strategies Across Heterogeneous Architectures

claim: CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts and CyclicLR outperform basic learning rate decay strategies
conditions: 9 PyTorch scheduler families, CIFAR-10, mixed CNN and transformer architectures
effect: Modern cyclic/restart schedulers achieve higher accuracy than classical decay
evidence: Direct comparison across 3,938 model variants
quote: CosineAnnealingWarmRestarts and CyclicLR consistently outperform basic decay strategies.
paper: Systematic Evaluation of Learning Rate Scheduling Strategies Across Heterogeneous Architectures

claim: Best empirical configuration achieves 86.45% top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10; 237 of 3,938 variants exceed 80%
conditions: CIFAR-10 classification, 30 architectures, 25 scheduler configurations, single training run per configuration
effect: 80%+ accuracy is achievable on CIFAR-10 with systematic scheduler selection
evidence: Direct experimental results on standard benchmark
quote: Our best configuration achieved a top-1 accuracy of 86.45%, with 237 variants exceeding 80%.
paper: Systematic Evaluation of Learning Rate Scheduling Strategies Across Heterogeneous Architectures

claim: UBA schedule shows particular effectiveness at constrained iteration budgets (25% and 50% of full epochs)
conditions: CIFAR-100 and ImageNet with ResNet architectures, multiple epoch budgets
effect: UBA consistently outperforms at 25% and 50% budgets, demonstrating budget efficiency
evidence: Comparative experimental evaluation across datasets and architectures
quote: (ii) UBA outperforms baselines not only at 100% training budget but also at 25% and 50% iteration budgets, demonstrating its budget efficiency, i.e. effectiveness in computation-constrained scenarios.
paper: Stepsize anything: A unified learning rate schedule for budgeted-iteration training

claim: Learning rate schedule design fundamentally impacts accuracy achievable under fixed iteration budgets, as evidenced by UBA's consistent superiority across diverse architectures and datasets
conditions: Vision tasks (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet) with ResNet18/34/50, multiple epoch budgets
effect: UBA achieves measurable accuracy gains across small-scale (CIFAR) and large-scale (ImageNet) benchmarks relative to alternative schedules
evidence: Comprehensive experimental comparison in Table 2 across all dataset and budget combinations
quote: We find that: (i) UBA demonstrates the strongest performance across all training budgets, achieving superior results on both small-scale (CIFAR10/100 with ResNet18/34) and large-scale (ImageNet with ResNet50) benchmarks. This consistent improvement highlights the generalizability across model and dataset scales.
paper: Stepsize anything: A unified learning rate schedule for budgeted-iteration training

claim: CIFAR-100 ResNet-56 at 25 epochs with 1cycle (0.1-0.5) learning rate exceeds accuracy of any step learning rate policy result at any epoch count
conditions: CIFAR-100, ResNet-56, batch size 512, 1cycle policy vs step policy, 25 epochs
effect: Faster convergence: 25 epochs with 1cycle beats all step-policy epoch counts
evidence: Table 2 comparison and text statement
quote: at only 25 epochs the accuracy is higher than any with a step learning rate policy
paper: Super-Convergence: Very Fast Training of Neural Networks Using Large Learning Rates

claim: Wider architectures (Wide ResNet) converge faster with 1cycle: 96.5% in 100 epochs versus 95.3% with standard step policy requiring 800 epochs
conditions: CIFAR-10 Wide ResNet 32, batch size 512, LR range 0.1-1.0, 100 vs 800 epochs
effect: 8x fewer epochs for comparable accuracy on wider networks
evidence: Table 2 and text discussion of wide resnets
quote: In 100 epochs, the wide32 network converges and provides a test accuracy of while the standard training method achieves an accuracy of only in 800 epochs
paper: Super-Convergence: Very Fast Training of Neural Networks Using Large Learning Rates

claim: Under budget restrictions, importance sampling approaches do not provide consistent improvement over uniform sampling
conditions: CIFAR-10/100, budget-restricted iterative training (e.g., 30% budget reduction)
effect: No consistent improvement; uniform sampling is as good or better
evidence: Empirical observation from comparative experiments on CIFAR-10/100
quote: We show that under budget restrictions, importance sampling approaches do not provide a consistent improvement over uniform sampling.
paper: How Important is Importance Sampling for Deep Budgeted Training?

claim: RICAP data augmentation maintains accuracy when budget is reduced to 30% on CIFAR-10/100
conditions: CIFAR-10/100, 30% budget reduction, RICAP data augmentation applied
effect: Accuracy is maintained (specific magnitude not stated in abstract)
evidence: Experimental comparison on CIFAR-10/100 under budget constraints
quote: when reducing the budget to a 30% in CIFAR-10/100, RICAP data augmentation maintains accuracy, while importance sampling does not.
paper: How Important is Importance Sampling for Deep Budgeted Training?

claim: Under budget restrictions, introducing adequate data augmentation is more effective than importance sampling for maintaining accuracy
conditions: Deep neural networks under budget constraints (e.g., 30% budget reduction on CIFAR-10/100)
effect: Maintains or recovers accuracy more effectively than sample-importance approaches
evidence: Empirical finding from comparison of augmentation vs. importance sampling strategies
quote: We suggest that, given a specific budget, the best course of action is to disregard the importance and introduce adequate data augmentation
paper: How Important is Importance Sampling for Deep Budgeted Training?

claim: DNNs under budget restrictions benefit from variety in the training set more than from optimal sample selection
conditions: Budget-constrained DNN training, balancing high performance with low computational requirements
effect: Variety in training set is more effective for performance than finding the 'right' samples to train on
evidence: Conclusion from empirical work comparing sampling strategies vs. augmentation/diversity
quote: DNNs under budget restrictions benefit greatly from variety in the training set and that finding the right samples to train on is not the most effective strategy when balancing high performance with low computational requirements.
paper: How Important is Importance Sampling for Deep Budgeted Training?

claim: EfficientNetV2-S achieves the highest observed top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-100 at 86.98%
conditions: CIFAR-100, EfficientNetV2-S, full training (unspecified epoch count), presumably with TTA (not explicitly stated)
effect: 86.98% top-1 accuracy
evidence: Comparative benchmark study across lightweight CNNs
quote: EfficientNetV2-S achieves the highest observed top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 at 97.57% and 86.98%
paper: Do Newer Lightweight CNNs Perform Better Under Resource Constraints? A Controlled Multigenerational Study of Architecture, Initialization, Training Budget, and Efficiency

claim: EfficientNet-B0 is within 0.85 percentage points of the best CIFAR-100 result while using approximately 79% fewer parameters and 86% fewer GMACs than EfficientNetV2-S
conditions: CIFAR-100, EfficientNet-B0, full training (unspecified epochs), reduced parameters and computation
effect: ~86.13% top-1 accuracy (0.85 pp below 86.98% best), 79% fewer parameters, 86% fewer GMACs
evidence: Comparative benchmark study
quote: EfficientNet-B0 remains within 0.22, 0.85, and 1.79 percentage points of the best result on the three datasets while using approximately 79% fewer parameters and 86% fewer GMACs than EfficientNetV2-S
paper: Do Newer Lightweight CNNs Perform Better Under Resource Constraints? A Controlled Multigenerational Study of Architecture, Initialization, Training Budget, and Efficiency

claim: EfficientNet-B0 remains 10.10 percentage points below its pretrained counterpart after 100 epochs of scratch training on CIFAR-100
conditions: CIFAR-100, EfficientNet-B0, 100 epochs from-scratch training (longer than the 8.5 epochs of E001)
effect: ~76.9% top-1 accuracy after 100 epochs scratch (if pretrained is ~86.98%)
evidence: Controlled training comparison with pretrained baseline
quote: EfficientNet-B0 remains 3.29, 10.10, and 17.54 points below its pretrained counterpart after 100 epochs of scratch training, despite requiring about five times the recorded training time
paper: Do Newer Lightweight CNNs Perform Better Under Resource Constraints? A Controlled Multigenerational Study of Architecture, Initialization, Training Budget, and Efficiency

claim: MobileNetV3-Small leads MobileNetV4-Conv-S by 1.76 percentage points on CIFAR-100 under random initialization with paired test-set intervals excluding zero
conditions: CIFAR-100, MobileNetV3-Small vs MobileNetV4-Conv-S, random initialization (from-scratch), full training
effect: 1.76 pp accuracy advantage for MobileNetV3-Small
evidence: Controlled comparison with statistical significance (paired test-set intervals excluding zero)
quote: Under random initialization, it leads MobileNetV4-Conv-S by 2.55, 1.76, and 0.99 points, with paired test-set intervals excluding zero for the fixed trained models
paper: Do Newer Lightweight CNNs Perform Better Under Resource Constraints? A Controlled Multigenerational Study of Architecture, Initialization, Training Budget, and Efficiency

claim: Optimizer choice (AdamW vs SGD) with mixed-precision training yields measurable accuracy gains
conditions: ResNet-18 and MobileNetV2 on CIFAR-10, 100 epochs, NVIDIA RTX 3060 Ti, validation accuracy metric
effect: 1.5–2.5 percentage point improvement in validation accuracy
evidence: Experimental comparison across 6 optimizer × precision configurations
quote: AdamW with PyTorch AMP reduced per-epoch training time by 29–31 % relative to SGD FP32 while improving validation accuracy by 1.5–2.5 percentage points.
paper: COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS OF OPTIMIZATION ALGORITHMS AND MIXED-PRECISION TRAINING FOR MINIMIZING NEURAL NETWORK TRAINING TIME

claim: Progressive image size increase during training accelerates training but reduces accuracy
conditions: Image classification (ImageNet, CIFAR, Cars, Flowers datasets); supervised training with convolutional networks
effect: Training speed improvement; accuracy drop occurs
evidence: Empirical results from EfficientNetV2 training experiments on multiple datasets
quote: Our training can be further sped up by progressively increasing the image size during training, but it often causes a drop in accuracy.
paper: EfficientNetV2: Smaller Models and Faster Training

claim: Adaptive regularization adjustment (dropout, data augmentation) recovers accuracy lost from progressive image size scheduling
conditions: Progressive image size training schedule on ImageNet/CIFAR/Cars/Flowers; supervised training with convolutional networks
effect: Eliminates accuracy drop from progressive learning while retaining training speed gains; achieves both fast training and high accuracy
evidence: Empirical validation on multiple datasets showing EfficientNetV2 outperforms prior models under progressive learning strategy
quote: To compensate for this accuracy drop, we propose to adaptively adjust regularization (e.g., dropout and data augmentation) as well, such that we can achieve both fast training and good accuracy.
paper: EfficientNetV2: Smaller Models and Faster Training

claim: Image resizing techniques improve classification accuracy
conditions: Histopathology image classification with DCNN on multiclass tumor classification (74 brain tumor types)
effect: 15-28% accuracy improvement
evidence: Empirical results on multiple datasets and architectures
quote: LRET consistently outperforms existing methods, yielding a substantial improvement of 15-28% in accuracy for a large-scale, multiclass tumor classification task consisting of 74 distinct brain tumor types.
paper: Learned Image resizing with efficient training (LRET) facilitates improved performance of large-scale digital histopathology image classification models

claim: Coupling resizing with efficient training reduces training time
conditions: Histopathology image classification with multiple DCNN architectures
effect: Substantially reduced training times
evidence: Empirical observation across multiple experiments
quote: LRET not only elevates classification accuracy but also substantially reduces training times, unlocking the potential for faster model development and iteration.
paper: Learned Image resizing with efficient training (LRET) facilitates improved performance of large-scale digital histopathology image classification models

claim: Learned resizing preserves structural information while integrating larger image patches
conditions: Histopathology image classification with multiple datasets and architectures
effect: Enable seamless integration of larger patches without information loss
evidence: Method design principle; empirical validation through performance gains
quote: Our method, termed Learned Resizing with Efficient Training (LRET), couples efficient training techniques with image resizing to facilitate seamless integration of larger histology image patches into state-of-the-art classification models while preserving important structural information.
paper: Learned Image resizing with efficient training (LRET) facilitates improved performance of large-scale digital histopathology image classification models

claim: Using interpolation kernels for downsampling without proper anti-aliasing filtering causes visual artifacts
conditions: Image downsampling operations; typical interpolation kernels (bilinear, cubic)
effect: Unspecified visual degradation; industry practice shows this mistake is common
evidence: Qualitative observation of industry practice and recommendations
quote: For instance, even in commercial products we find the mistake of using interpolation kernels for downsampling without the necessary lowpass filtering.
paper: New Filters for Image Interpolation and Resizing

claim: Insufficient spectrum attenuation during downsampling causes 'screen door' effect
conditions: Downsampling with filters that don't adequately remove periodic spectrum repetitions
effect: Visible aliasing artifacts (screen door effect) in output images
evidence: Visual demonstration with example image (Figure 4c) showing the artifact
quote: Another problem occurs when the filters do not remove enough of the periodic versions in the spectrum of the sampled signal. In this case we have the "screen door" effect, as shown in Figure 4 (c).
paper: New Filters for Image Interpolation and Resizing

claim: Linear interpolation kernels applied to downsampling produce DC response errors that oscillate with resampling offset
conditions: Linear interpolation (tent function) used for downsampling; varying resampling offsets; ratio > 1
effect: ~20% oscillation in output values (±10% from ground truth) when offset = 0
evidence: Mathematical analysis with quantified measurements shown in Figure 10-11
quote: In fact, in the latter case, if the resampling offset is zero, then the sampled response will alternate between values that are about 10% too large, and 10% too small, i.e., an oscillation of about 20%!
paper: New Filters for Image Interpolation and Resizing

claim: Different downsampling kernels produce measurably different output quality
conditions: Downsampling by factor 0.6; natural images with fine detail (JPEG2000 'Bike' test image)
effect: PSNR differences of 2-19 dB between different kernels; visual quality varies but all produce acceptable results
evidence: Quantitative PSNR measurements comparing Lanczos (LZ4), Blackman-Harris (BH6), and cubic B-spline (CBS) kernels
quote: The values in the main diagonal show that the images obtained with the kernels and their approximations are indeed very close. The other values are also large, indicating that all those kernels produce good results, but the differences are also clear.
paper: New Filters for Image Interpolation and Resizing

claim: Fast frequency-domain decay in kernels reduces DC response error during downsampling
conditions: Downsampling operations; kernels with fast asymptotic decay in both time and frequency domains
effect: Nearly constant DC response error across all resampling offsets (≤2% error shown in Figure 14-15)
evidence: Frequency response analysis and measured DC response errors comparing proposed kernels to standard interpolation kernels
quote: As explained in Section 5.5 , an advantage of the new kernels is that they present very fast decays on the frequency response, which can make them (depending on the parameters) better for downsizing because of the smaller error on the DC response.
paper: New Filters for Image Interpolation and Resizing

claim: Progressive resolution training (64×64 to 96×96) enables faster convergence
conditions: CIFAR-10 dataset, UltraLight+ CNN architecture (75,530 parameters), multi-phase progressive training, 1.05MB final model size
effect: Faster convergence (magnitude unquantified); maintains efficient deployment
evidence: Experimental demonstration via progressive training protocol; not an isolated ablation or comparative study of resolution schedules
quote: The progressive training protocol, which transitions from 64×64 to 96×96 resolution, enables faster convergence and maintains efficient deployment with a 1.05MB model size.
paper: UltraLight+: An Optimized Progressive CNN Architecture for Efficient Image Classification

claim: Dynamic resolution scaling combined with multi-phase training reduces parameters while improving accuracy vs. baseline
conditions: CIFAR-10, UltraLight+ architecture with dynamic resolution scaling and multi-phase training; comparison baseline: MobileNetV2 (0.35α)
effect: 79.6% accuracy on CIFAR-10, 82% parameter reduction vs. MobileNetV2 (75,530 vs. ~427k params), 79% higher accuracy (44.4% → 79.6%)
evidence: Experimental comparison; effect is confounded with architecture changes and other optimizations (hybrid depthwise-separable convolutions, adaptive feature fusion)
quote: Our approach combines dynamic resolution scaling with multi-phase training and introduces hybrid depthwise-separable convolution blocks with adaptive feature fusion mechanisms. UltraLight+ achieves 79.6% accuracy on CIFAR-10 with only 75,530 parameters, representing an 82% parameter reduction compared to MobileNetV2 (0.35α) while delivering 79% higher accuracy (44.4% vs 79.6%).
paper: UltraLight+: An Optimized Progressive CNN Architecture for Efficient Image Classification

claim: Performance improves predictably with training time, dataset size, and model size across many orders of magnitude
conditions: Neural networks on a variety of tasks, trained with gradient descent
effect: Consistent improvement in performance across three independent scaling axes
evidence: Empirical observation across multiple domains (general scaling law phenomenon)
quote: On a variety of tasks, the performance of neural networks predictably improves with training time, dataset size and model size across many orders of magnitude.
paper: A Dynamical Model of Neural Scaling Laws

claim: Scaling of performance with training time and model size follow different power law exponents
conditions: Random feature model trained with gradient descent; applicable to network training generally
effect: Asymmetric scaling relationships: time and model size contribute unequally to performance gains
evidence: Theoretical prediction from solvable random feature model
quote: First, our model makes a prediction about why the scaling of performance with training time and with model size have different power law exponents.
paper: A Dynamical Model of Neural Scaling Laws

claim: Asymmetric compute-optimal scaling rule: training steps should be increased faster than model parameters
conditions: Compute-optimal regime; assumes fixed computational budget
effect: At fixed compute, greater improvements from increasing steps than from increasing model width
evidence: Theory consistent with recent empirical observations
quote: Consequently, the theory predicts an asymmetric compute-optimal scaling rule where the number of training steps are increased faster than model parameters, consistent with recent empirical observations.
paper: A Dynamical Model of Neural Scaling Laws

claim: Convergence rate to infinite-width dynamics transitions from width-independent (1/width) early in training to width-dependent (width^-c) late in training
conditions: Neural network training; transition occurs between early and late training phases; c depends on architecture and task structure
effect: Width effects on learning dynamics change in magnitude and form over training
evidence: Theoretical model exhibiting this behavior; observations from prior work
quote: Second, it has been observed that early in training, networks converge to their infinite-width dynamics at a rate $1/\textit{width}$ but at late time exhibit a rate $\textit{width}^{-c}$, where $c$ depends on the structure of the architecture and task.
paper: A Dynamical Model of Neural Scaling Laws

claim: Training-test loss gap grows over time due to repeated reuse of the same data
conditions: Finite dataset, multiple training epochs causing data reuse
effect: Generalization gap accumulates with training duration independent of model capacity
evidence: Theoretical analysis showing how data reuse affects the gap
quote: Lastly, our theory shows how the gap between training and test loss can gradually build up over time due to repeated reuse of data.
paper: A Dynamical Model of Neural Scaling Laws

claim: Optimal scaling strategy is critically task-dependent; generation requires data size to grow 3-5× faster than classification optimal setups
conditions: Image classification vs. generation tasks at fixed resolution (32×32)
effect: Generation requires 3-5× faster data scaling rate than classification for equivalent performance
evidence: Empirical finding from scaling experiments across compute budgets up to 7e19 FLOPs
quote: optimal scaling strategy is critically task-dependent. At a fixed resolution of 32x32 alone, the optimal scaling properties for image classification and image generation diverge, where generation optimal setup requires the data size grow three to five times faster than for the classification optimal setup.
paper: Rethinking Generative Image Pretraining: How Far Are We From Scaling Up Next-Pixel Prediction?

claim: As image resolution increases, model size must grow much faster than data size in the optimal scaling strategy
conditions: Increasing image resolution from 32×32 baseline
effect: Model capacity scaling must outpace data size scaling; non-linear relationship between model width and data requirements
evidence: Empirical finding from multi-resolution scaling experiments
quote: as image resolution increases, the optimal scaling strategy indicates that the model size must grow much faster than data size.
paper: Rethinking Generative Image Pretraining: How Far Are We From Scaling Up Next-Pixel Prediction?

claim: The primary bottleneck limiting performance is compute rather than training data quantity
conditions: Scaling experiments across full compute budget range (up to 7e19 FLOPs)
effect: Performance gains are compute-limited; increasing data without proportional compute gains yields diminishing returns
evidence: Projection and finding from scaling study across compute budgets
quote: the primary bottleneck is compute rather than the amount of training data.
paper: Rethinking Generative Image Pretraining: How Far Are We From Scaling Up Next-Pixel Prediction?

claim: Training throughput exhibits a non-monotonic relationship with batch size, peaking at an optimal value and then declining; this throughput ceiling is distinct from inference which monotonically improves with larger batch sizes.
conditions: ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10/100 and TinyImageNet; edge CPU devices (Raspberry Pi 4, Jetson Xavier, Banana Pi, ZCU102); gradient-based training with backpropagation
effect: Optimal batch size achieves ≥1.25× throughput improvement over maximum batch size (peaks ~2× on Raspberry Pi); throughput degrades beyond optimal point
evidence: Empirical measurement across devices and datasets; comparison of training vs. inference throughput curves
quote: a distinct pattern emerges across all edge devices where the training throughput peaks and subsequently declines as the batch size increases. This phenomenon represents a throughput ceiling, where hardware reaches its maximum processing rate for a given input batch size.
paper: TASTE: Throughput-Aware Batch Size Tuning for On-Device Edge Learning

claim: The throughput ceiling in training is caused by memory overhead from storing intermediate activations required for backpropagation, which scales with batch size. Inference lacks this constraint and thus does not exhibit a throughput ceiling.
conditions: ResNet-18 training with gradient computation; backward pass dependency on intermediate layer activations
effect: Training throughput begins declining when batch size exceeds memory-optimal point; inference throughput continues improving with larger batches
evidence: Direct mechanistic explanation comparing training vs. inference computational graphs and memory requirements
quote: The bottleneck is due to the need to store intermediate activations from the ResNet-18 layers required for the backward pass, which scales with the batch size. In contrast, inference does not require the retention of intermediate activations.
paper: TASTE: Throughput-Aware Batch Size Tuning for On-Device Edge Learning

claim: Final and later layers of CNNs require disproportionately higher channel counts than earlier layers to achieve optimal accuracy
conditions: ImageNet classification with ResNet18 and MobileNetV2 architectures; width optimization across DMCP, AutoSlim, and MorphNet algorithms
effect: Optimized networks expand final layer widths dramatically—ResNet18 from 512→1300 channels (~2.5×); MobileNetV2 from 1280→3785 channels (~3×)
evidence: Empirical measurement via width optimization experiments across three state-of-the-art algorithms; visualization in Figure 5
quote: We find that the later layers tend to increase a lot compared to the un-optimized ones. Concretely, in un-optimized networks, ResNet18 has 512 channels in the last layer and MobileNetV2 has 1280 channels in the last layer. In contrast, the average optimized width has 1300 channels for ResNet18 and 3785 channels for MobileNetV2.
paper: Width Transfer: On the (In)variance of Width Optimization

claim: Width optimization produces scale-invariant patterns within network stages; relative widths within a stage transfer reliably across different network depths
conditions: Network width optimization on ImageNet; depth multipliers {1,2,3,4}; ResNet18 and MobileNetV2; all three width optimization algorithms (DMCP, AutoSlim, MorphNet)
effect: ~75% width optimization overhead reduction while preserving accuracy; layer stacking strategies (stack-average-block, stack-last-block) reliably transfer patterns across depth variations
evidence: Experiments in Section 4.3; Figure 4(c)-(d); empirical validation across compound projections; controlled experiments with three random seeds
quote: In other words, the pattern of width multipliers across depth is scale-invariant.
paper: Width Transfer: On the (In)variance of Width Optimization

claim: Non-uniform narrowing across blocks without maintaining coordinated width relationships across stages causes accuracy degradation beyond isolated block-level predictions
conditions: Width optimization with block-level width changes; ImageNet classification; resolution and architecture projection experiments; MorphNet, AutoSlim, and DMCP algorithms
effect: MorphNet transferred from low resolution (64px) to ResNet18 shows substantial accuracy loss compared to direct optimization; demonstrates that block-structure coherence is required for maintaining accuracy
evidence: Experiment in Section 4.4; Figure 7(a); comparison of optimized widths across different resolutions shown in Appendix similarity analysis; mismatch between transferred and directly-optimized architectures
quote: Interestingly, we find that MorphNet had a very different optimized widths when transferred from resolution 64 for ResNet18, which leads to the worse performance for ResNet18 compared to direct optimization.
paper: Width Transfer: On the (In)variance of Width Optimization

claim: Careful architectural design allows simultaneous increases in depth and width while maintaining a constant computational budget
conditions: Deep convolutional neural networks for ImageNet ILSVRC 2014 classification and detection tasks
effect: Enables efficient scaling of network capacity without proportional increases in computational cost
evidence: Stated architectural principle of the Inception/GoogLeNet design
quote: a carefully crafted design that allows for increasing the depth and width of the network while keeping the computational budget constant
paper: Going Deeper with Convolutions

claim: Multi-scale processing through parallel convolutional paths improves model quality
conditions: ImageNet classification/detection with deep convolutional architectures
effect: Improved accuracy through multi-scale feature extraction
evidence: Stated design principle and architectural choice
quote: architectural decisions were based on the Hebbian principle and the intuition of multi-scale processing
paper: Going Deeper with Convolutions

claim: Improved utilization of computing resources inside the network is the main mechanism for achieving state-of-the-art results
conditions: Deep CNN architecture for ImageNet ILSVRC 2014
effect: State-of-the-art classification and detection performance
evidence: Main hallmark stated as driving performance improvement
quote: The main hallmark of this architecture is the improved utilization of the computing resources inside the network
paper: Going Deeper with Convolutions

claim: Network depth (measured in number of layers) is a critical factor for performance
conditions: ImageNet classification/detection; GoogLeNet architecture with 22 layers
effect: Enabled competitive state-of-the-art results in ILSVRC 2014
evidence: Empirical result from competition submission
quote: a 22 layers deep network, the quality of which is assessed in the context of classification and detection
paper: Going Deeper with Convolutions

claim: Optimal hyperparameters change substantially with training horizon (overtraining factor)
conditions: Multiple optimizers (AdamW, Muon, SOAP, ADANA), models 51M–253M parameters, OT factors 1x–256x, base learning rate swept at every setting
effect: Relative optimizer performance and optimal hyperparameters vary substantially—not constant across horizons
evidence: Empirical study across model scales and overtraining factors
quote: relative optimizer performance and optimal hyperparameters change substantially with training horizon
paper: Optimizer Memory Schedules for Outscaling the Overtraining Axis

claim: Preferred learning rate schedule reverses across the overtraining axis
conditions: Same study setup: multiple optimizers, models 51M–253M, OT factors 1x–256x
effect: Complete inversion of which schedule is optimal at different training horizons
evidence: Empirical observation across the measured overtraining range
quote: The preferred learning rate schedule can reverse across the overtraining axis
paper: Optimizer Memory Schedules for Outscaling the Overtraining Axis

claim: Best weight decay coefficient scales approximately as sqrt(OT)
conditions: Measured across multiple optimizers, OT factors 1x–256x
effect: Weight decay should increase as the square root of the overtraining factor
evidence: Empirical measurement across overtraining range
quote: the best weight decay coefficient scales approximately as sqrt(OT)
paper: Optimizer Memory Schedules for Outscaling the Overtraining Axis

claim: Longer training horizons generally favor longer fixed memory in the optimizer
conditions: Study of memory-based optimizers (Muon, SOAP, ADANA) across OT factors 1x–256x
effect: Momentum/memory window should increase as training horizon increases
evidence: Empirical finding across optimizer variants and overtraining factors
quote: longer horizons generally favor longer fixed memory
paper: Optimizer Memory Schedules for Outscaling the Overtraining Axis
